#8728. Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

There are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

If you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

“The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, says Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

The textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

All things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin says. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

Regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin says.

Because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin says. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, says Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

And it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin says. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

Home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin says. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”

That’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health issues.

If left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, says Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really quickly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra says, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

Because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition issues and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar says. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research shows that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

As researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s important to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

#8727. 7 Common Misdiagnoses for Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS)

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a skin condition that often gets caught up in a case of mistaken identity in a lineup of suspects. Specifically, people confuse HS for some more common conditions.

With their host of bumps, rashes, flakiness, or scales, skin conditions can sometimes be tricky to diagnose. That’s because they often share common symptoms or have symptoms that overlap with or mimic those of another skin issue.

So, what exactly is HS? It’s a chronic, progressive skin condition that typically appears as boil-like lumps in friction-prone and sweaty areas, where your skin can be sensitive. These lumps can form interconnected tracts underneath your skin (aka “tunneling”) that may become irritated or even infected.

Knowing how the symptoms of HS compare with those of other inflammatory skin conditions can help you advocate for the correct diagnosis and care, which is crucial for staving off disease progression.

Here are 7 conditions that HS commonly gets mistaken for.

HS isn’t rare — it affects up to 4% of the population. But by comparison, acne vulgaris affects more than more than 9% of people worldwide. Sometimes HS can be mistaken for acne simply because acne is more common. But these two conditions are quite different.

Acne typically shows up as papules, pustules, or nodules, which are commonly called zits or blemishes. Acne most often appears on your face but can also affect your back, chest, arms, and buttocks. It occurs when your sebaceous glands have a hypersensitivity to circulating androgens (like testosterone).

By comparison, HS most often appears in sweat- and friction-prone areas, such as your armpits or groin. It occurs when hair follicles become blocked — though more research is needed to learn what causes these blockages.

Acne conglobata (AC) is a rare but intense form of nodulocystic acne. With AC, the cysts and nodules connect under your skin, and this can lead to infections and scarring. Since AC features a “tunneling” effect that may appear similar to HS, many people confuse these two otherwise distinct conditions.

One key difference? HS often appears in areas that are subjected to friction from skin-on-skin contact or chafing. AC, on the other hand, can appear anywhere on your body. To further complicate things, many people with HS also have AC, and some research suggests a link between the two conditions.

A cyst is a fluid-filled sac. Cysts have many possible causes, including injuries and minor infections. They often go away on their own, but some may require treatment.

HS bumps can resemble cysts — but HS is an ongoing inflammatory condition.

An ingrown hair happens when a strand of hair anywhere on your body grows into your skin instead of out. Ingrown hairs commonly occur after shaving, waxing, or tweezing. After hair removal, a tiny new hair can curl inward, creating a bump (often called a razor bump).

Sometimes people confuse HS bumps for ingrown hairs — especially since HS often occurs in places where hair removal is common, such as the armpits and bikini area. Another confusing factor is that HS develops from blocked follicles. However, the cause of the blockage in HS is more complicated than an ingrown hair.

Folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles, usually caused by a bacterial infection. The inflamed hair follicles show up as small bumps and can look like ingrown hairs.

People commonly mistake HS for folliculitis because the conditions often occur in the same skin areas.

Mild folliculitis tends to go away on its own with at-home treatment, though more severe forms may require antibiotics. HS, on the other hand, is a chronic condition.

A boil (also called a furuncle) is a bump filled with pus. The bump develops from a bacterial infection, often of a hair follicle. The infection causes a buildup of immune and skin cells, which leads to the formation of the bump. A carbuncle is a cluster of boils.

People often confuse HS with boils. However, boils are the result of an infection, and proper treatment typically resolves the issue. Meanwhile, the boil-like bumps of HS often require ongoing treatment.

Herpes is a common sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the herpes simplex virus. It shows up as painful sores or blisters.

Since herpes often affects the genital area and HS occurs around the groin or bikini line, people may confuse the two conditions. But while herpes can be spread through direct contact, HS is not contagious.

Other skin conditions can mimic HS, and vice versa. But a misdiagnosis can lead to an incorrect treatment that won’t actually ease your symptoms or slow the condition’s progression. This is true for other skin conditions as well.

That’s why, if you have symptoms of any of the above conditions, you should talk with a knowledgeable dermatologist who can properly diagnose your concerns and find the right treatment plan.

Last medically reviewed on February 14, 2025

A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that currently average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

Right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

Timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

This is the most important financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Users Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare Users Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

Timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

Pro tip: Pay the balance in full every month. Travel rewards only work financially if you never carry a balance and pay interest.

Instead of paying $1,120/year in mandatory timeshare fees, deposit that same amount monthly ($93/month) into a high-yield savings account earmarked for travel. You'll have $1,120+ per year to spend on any vacation, anywhere.

Research destinations on Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com. Booking 3-6 months ahead gets the best selection. Compare total costs including cleaning fees and service charges to timeshare equivalent costs.

Shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

If you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

Pro tip: Set up automatic monthly investments for the amount you would have spent on timeshare financing payments.

A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

No. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

The average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

Technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

The resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

Some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

In very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.

#8725. Four Projects in Thailand and Indonesia Recognized at the Steel Architectural Awards ASEAN 2026

An innovation campus, a corporate headquarters, a family home, and a community development in a remote peatland environment are the four winners of the Steel Architectural Awards ASEAN 2026. Located in Thailand and Indonesia, the projects explore how coated steel can respond to different climates, construction conditions, and patterns of use. The winners were announced at the ASEAN Awards Ceremony in Bangkok, Thailand, on November 20, 2026. They were selected from 12 finalists representing Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam, following awards programs in each country.

Under the theme "Shaping Resilient Futures: Timeless Design with Coated Steel," the awards examined how architectural ideas, construction details, and material choices contribute to a building's capacity to remain in use over time. Entries were assessed on their response to context and climate, technical resolution, innovation, and long-term material performance. Design Excellence accounted for 50% of the evaluation, Innovation for 30%, and Sustainability for 20%.

#8724. London Museum brings "back a bit of London's heritage" with Smithfield Market opening

Architecture studios Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have completed their long-awaited transformation of the 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum.

Opening to the public on Saturday, the former Victorian market hall now functions as a museum that tells the story of London’s history through exhibitions designed by German studio Atelier Brückner.

According to the London Museum, it is the largest dedicated city museum in the world.

Ten years in the making, the opening of Smithfield General Market marks the first phase of the London Museum’s relocation from the Barbican Estate’s former Museum of London, which is set to be demolished.

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have overhauled the General Market, which fell into disrepair after it closed in the 1990s, and will also convert the adjacent 1960s Poultry Market, which is expected to open in 2028.

“There’s an opportunity to represent London as it is now and in the future, and really take city museums to another level,” said London Museum’s New Museum Project director Alec Shaw.

“We’re bringing back a bit of London’s heritage – one building that has not been seen or encountered for at least 30 years, and the other one an amazing architectural gem that hasn’t been fully appreciated and will now be,” he told Dezeen.

The main entrance to the London Museum is marked by a covered street, West Poultry Avenue, which doubles as the Real Time gallery that stretches between the General Market and Poultry Market.

Entering the transformed Victorian market, visitors pass a museum shop and an auditorium before entering Our Time – an expansive gallery illuminated from above by an oculus.

Shops that once wrapped the perimeter of the market trading floor were removed to open up the space, but the restoration was designed to retain hints of the building fabric’s history.

“You can see pockets in the brickwork walls where joists of the first floor and little plaster columns were originally located,” said Julian Harrap Architects partner Lyall Thow.

“There was a second floor, represented by a darkened band where we didn’t overly clean the brickwork, and fireplaces in the upper offices were taken out, restored, and put back where they would have been originally.”

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects overhauled 42 individual shops that formerly encircled the General Market into 12 multi-storey units.

Six units were kept to contain a restaurant, galleries and learning spaces, while the other six were left for the museum to invite partner institutions to occupy.

“What the ‘museum of tomorrow’ will be is not just a single institute, but a coral reef of small institutes that can plug in – Dezeen could have an office here, a leather upholsterer might have a craft workshop here, restaurants and pop-ups…” said Khan.

“This living ecosystem, which is reflective of the city, is possible because of this market building we’ve moved into,” he continued.

“What we’ve done is make openings, windows, and cuts through the floor and ceiling, which allow that energy to emanate out of the city and for the city’s energy to emanate inwards,” added Khan. “At the centre of it all is this enormous public space, the General Market ground floor, where anything can happen.”

A staircase takes visitors down to London’s Roman street level, to the museum’s permanent Past Time exhibition, which displays precious artefacts.

The restored brickwork walls in the subterranean space are interrupted by a six-metre window, revealing passing Thameslink trains.

A series of underground vaults that were discovered during the museum’s construction will open to visitors in spring 2027.

“This museum epitomises the idea of the primordial reflex in us to dig to find various treasures,” said Stanton Williams co-founder Paul Williams.

The architects aimed to make the qualities of the existing spaces work to the museum’s advantage, displaying delicate objects in the underground gallery and maintaining the communal feel of the market space on ground level.

“Decisions based on the building – like precious objects should be kept underground because it’s got a greater thermal inertia – loosen the straitjacket around the museum having to act like a museum in other spaces,” said Khan.

“It means some other spaces can be more market-like and have a more public-facing potential that a normal museum wouldn’t be able to do,” he continued. “The building has enabled the museum to become a different kind of museum.”

Unisex toilets were designed in a Victorian style, with decorative tiles depicting wildflowers that grew in London’s bombed-out sites.

Elsewhere in the museum is a 24-hour cafe where original interior tiles and a timber staircase were restored.

Shaw hopes the London Museum will be an inviting place that residents and tourists want to return to time and again.

“We want to be super welcoming – we don’t want to be intimidating as a museum,” said Shaw. “Some of the other museums are quite imposing buildings.”

“We want to be a destination, not just a museum, but a place for people to keep coming back to.”

Other museums recently completed in London include V&A East by O’Donnell + Tuomey and the V&A East Storehouse by Diller Scofidio + Renfro, which was given a Dezeen Award for its wayfinding design.

#8723. Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s important to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about new plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

Plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

“It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she says.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

What that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

“There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he says. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”

About 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

And the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

“So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” says Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

In the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

At first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

“If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she says.

Part of the reason for this, says Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

Another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, says Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be important to find out for whom this works.”

As a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

“I would call this a phase 1 study,” says Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”

#8722. 7 Places on the Body That Hidradenitis Suppurativa Can Appear

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Despite what Instagram and photo filters would have us think, no one has perfectly smooth skin over the entirety of their body. We’re all prone to the occasional bump, rash, zit, or ingrown hair. These issues generally go away after the blocked follicle, clogged pore, or minor skin irritation resolves.

But hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is different. HS is a chronic, progressive skin condition that typically appears as boil-like lumps in some of your most sensitive regions (and beyond).

HS lumps or bumps can form interconnected tracts underneath the skin that may become inflamed and infected, causing discomfort and pain. Although infections are often a part of HS, the disease itself is not an infection — it’s due to an ongoing inflammatory response in the body.

In addition to causing pain and discomfort, HS can be extremely frustrating and impact your self-esteem. Identifying HS correctly and early is crucial for getting optimal care, easing symptoms, slowing disease progression, and improving your mental health.

While we don’t know what exactly causes HS, genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors may play a role. Skin regions prone to HS include those where we sweat often and where friction is super common. Friction can occur from skin rubbing on skin, or where clothing can chafe or rub.

Here are seven areas of the body that are often impacted by HS.

Our underarms are packed with hair follicles and apocrine glands (aka, sweat glands). With HS, these follicles and glands may become clogged, and bacteria can start to grow, leading to the inflamed boil-like bumps of HS.

If you’ve ever gone for a run and come back with the dreaded armpit chafing, you’re all too familiar with how this area of the body can be prone to skin-on-skin friction or excessive rubbing from clothing. (Lookin’ at you, sports bra!) Friction and chafing can also cause an HS flare-up.

Complicating matters is that some people shave or wax their armpits, and many understandably slather this region with antiperspirants or deodorants. These factors can also clog or irritate sweat glands and hair follicles.

The breasts, including underneath and even on the areolae (the area around the nipple), are a common place for HS to show up.

The breast area is a frequent spot for chafing from bras or other clothing. This chafing not only causes skin irritation — it can also trap sweat and bacteria on the skin. The areolae contain apocrine glands and hair follicles that can easily become infected. All these factors can contribute to an HS flare.

Research also points to sex hormones playing a role in HS, so a hormone shift or imbalance may also make breast tissue more prone to HS lesions. However, more research is needed on the connection between HS and hormones.

No one can deny that the crotch becomes a sweaty area when life gets steamy, either from the weather, a workout, or both. It’s also a common area for clothing to rub against just from walking and everyday movements.

As with other HS-prone areas, the groin and genital areas contain apocrine glands and oodles of hair follicles, all of which can become blocked as part of HS, leading to a flare. Speaking of hair down there, many people groom their pubic region, which can also lead to blocked hair follicles.

Again, hormonal shifts or imbalances may also play a role in why these sensitive areas can become hot spots for HS.

The inner thighs are an extension of the groin area. Similarly, sweat also hangs out here, and it’s a common spot for chafing to occur from skin-on-skin friction, or from clothing rubbing and irritating the area.

The entire buttocks area is also prone to HS in many people. Areas commonly affected include the anus, the butt crack, and the gluteal fold — or the crease where the buttocks meet the backs of the upper thighs.

Apocrine glands and hair follicles are abundant here, too. Sweat and other bacteria sources can also lead to HS infections. The buttocks are also subjected to pressure from sitting, which can lead to further irritation.

Although more research is needed, some studies suggest a link between HS and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). IBD is an umbrella term for conditions such as Crohn’s and ulcerative colitis. The potential links between HS and IBD may play a role in why the buttocks area is a common site for HS.

Although less common than in other areas, HS can also show up at the nape of the neck. This might be due to friction from clothing collars, jewelry, and other clothing or accessories. The neck is also a common site for sweat, which could block hair follicles in this area.

If skin folds at the waist, or clothing waistbands (especially tight ones!) cause friction, it can lead to HS in the waistband area. As a result, HS lesions may show up on the abdomen, back, or sides.

HS tends to appear on some of the body’s most sensitive places, including the underarms, breasts, groin, and buttocks. These areas are prone to sweat, friction, and irritation from hair removal — all of which may contribute to an HS flare.

If you suspect you have HS, talk with a knowledgeable dermatologist who can give you a proper diagnosis and help you develop the right treatment and self-care plan to combat irritation and flares so you can feel more comfortable in your skin.

Last medically reviewed on February 28, 2025

#8721. Grand Terminal Doha / Hassell

Text description provided by the architects. The Grand Terminal provides berths for two megaships, which can enjoy a variety of leisure and cultural amenities offered by the impressive waterside complex. Hassell Principal and Head of Design Ashley Munday said, "We are really excited that our Grand Terminal is beginning its life as a festival venue for the World Cup, but what excites us even more is its future as a loved piece of the city, embedded in the cultural fabric of Doha. It is a building that doesn't just have a singular function as a cruise terminal, but has been designed to absorb other uses during the year, like markets, exhibitions, and festivals. For us, this is a civic project that has to respond to many complex needs and requirements at once, but still has an 'outward' role to face the world and welcome people into a place that is really just emerging as a destination."

#8720. Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging architect of the year Kuma&Elsa

This year Kuma&Elsa was named emerging architect of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, they select five projects that demonstrate the ethos of the studio.

Led by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French-Spanish urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa has completed a wide variety of projects from their bases in France and Japan.

“We believe it is important not to impose a common consistency across our projects,” Kuma told Dezeen.

“Every project is unique, shaped by a one-off combination of site and client. Preserving that uniqueness requires an open mind. Personally, I quickly lose interest when things are planned in advance.”

“That said, there are certain topics, many of which are shared by our generation, such as feminism, the care for natural resources and a shared public space, that interest us on a personal level, and I imagine they find their way into our work,” added Escobedo.

“We try to approach them with a sense of joy.”

Although they have already designed a wide range of projects, from installations to houses and public toilets, the duo would like to work on more varied schemes and unusual projects, along with completing their own, long-running renovation.

“It would be nice to actually finish this self-renovation project at some point…” said Escobedo.

“More seriously, I’d love to experiment with the reuse of materials on a larger scale, or in a European context, working with European craftspeople.”

“I would love to work on overlooked building types and uses, especially those that have little place in architectural history and attract few expectations,” added Kuma. “Designing a toilet pavilion for the Expo, a building type that nobody expects to become architecture, is one example.”

Along with the variety in projects, both architects agreed that the wide range of daily activities is what they most enjoy about being an architect.

“The variety, the diversity,” said Escobedo, when asked about her favourite part about being an architect.

“One day you’re on a construction site with incredible Japanese carpenters, the next you’re discussing a detail with your favourite thermal engineer, the following week you’re taking part in a conversation with colleagues you admire, before finding yourself struggling to install the plumbing and tiles in a shower because you had the brilliant idea of taking on a self-build project.”

Kuma also added that he enjoys the intensity of working on site.

“The construction site,” he said. “Nothing is more stressful or demanding, with all the struggles involving people and money. Yet every time I see a building taking shape, I feel glad I chose architecture. There is something addictive about it.”

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning studio Kuma&Elsa, as described by the duo:

“The client’s childhood home, a traditional Japanese house, has an engawa gallery open to the garden. The new residence occupies the top two floors of a building owned by the client. She, along with her two sons and their families, will move into three apartments located on the sixth and seventh floors.

“At the centre of each apartment, we inserted a hut-like volume that gathers the quieter rooms: a small living room and the bedrooms. In the space carved out around it emerges an intermediate zone – an engawa that serves both as a place to stay and as a passage.

“Balcony, engawa, and hut thus form three spatial layers that resonate with the childhood home. The structure consists of Y-shaped modules made of lightweight steel sections and bracing cables, typically used in shelving systems.

“These modules are arranged two by two in mirrored pairs along a regular grid, with occasional inversions. From these new dwellings, one can look down across the street at the engawa of the childhood home. This project does not seek to nostalgically replicate that memory-laden place, but rather to build a new home nourished by the memories of the old one.”

“One water is a bathing and rest pavilion for the Osaka World Expo 2025. Toilets are at first glance a pragmatic facility, dedicated to human physiology. But they are also intimately linked to contemporary issues such as the use of natural resources and gender.

“One water uses the path of rainfall on the accessible roof and its subsequent accumulation to create encounters between water and the public, and contribute to the supply of the toilets.

“The design of the pavilion allows for the reuse of materials and structural components, and makes no gender distinction in the toilets, because, after all, ‘we are all fish in one water’.”

House by the temple, Saitama Prefecture, Japan, 2024

“The house is opposite the entrance of a temple that is surrounded by a park of ancient trees and a wall, as if it belongs to another world. Reflecting this closed composition, we designed the house as an everyday world for a family.

“The main building is located at the back of the plot and has a quarter-circle plan to reduce its own shadow. The street facade is a single-storey hut, which creates a continuity between the open space of the park and the garden of the house.

“On the ground floor, the park is the backdrop to the house. On the first floor, each room offers distant views of the temple, like an observatory.”

“A daily public space in a residential area. We create a plaza in a small residential area where human life is still at human scale.

“The house is like the background that forms the square. The composition consists of various couples: the smooth black mortar of the outer wall and the rough crushed black basalt ground, the emerald entrance hut and the crape myrtle tree with white flowers, the interior spaces and the outside square.”

Water Flower Courtyard, Montpellier, France, 2019

“The life of a flower is short: we wanted to express the fragility of a concentrated life from flowering to dispersal. This project was open to the public for a week during the Montpellier architecture festival Festival des Architectures Vives in June 2019.

“Eighteen lightweight units made of two-millimetre-thick aluminium sheets are laid out together as a forest.

“The tube is a vase that contains water and peony flowers, the bowl contains water and slate stones. All structures are self-supporting and their stability works as in a roly-poly toy. After a few days, petals start falling on the surface of the water.”

#8719. Does Your Building Work or Does It Just Photograph Well? What Neuroscience and Use Data Could Teach Architects

Architecture reaches people through whatever medium carries it, and each new medium changes our picture of what a good building looks like. For example, when 3D modeling software arrived, the novelty of complex shapes drove the starchitecture era of the 2010s, and projects built on those experiments earned awards such as the Pritzker Prize. Today the medium is the social media feed. A building exists first as a model and then as a render, long before it exists as a place. Meanwhile, research in neuroarchitecture is building a different picture based on how people actually experience buildings. So how could those two seemingly unrelated topics close a loop that may lead to the profession's next creative frontier?

Architecture reaches people through whatever medium carries it, and each new medium changes our picture of what a good building looks like. For example, when 3D modeling software arrived, the novelty of complex shapes drove the starchitecture era of the 2010s, and projects built on those experiments earned awards such as the Pritzker Prize. Today the medium is the social media feed. A building exists first as a model and then as a render, long before it exists as a place. Meanwhile, research in neuroarchitecture is building a different picture based on how people actually experience buildings. So how could those two seemingly unrelated topics close a loop that may lead to the profession's next creative frontier?

In the book Cognitive Architecture, Ann Sussman and Justin Hollander examine how the brain reacts to the built environment. In their research, people looked at photographs of buildings while their eye movements were tracked. Viewers tended to skip blank, featureless facades but lingered on details, contrast, and other people. One case study, the Stapleton Library in New York, shows how much fenestration patterns matter: windows provide areas of contrast that the eye seeks out and stays with. Their study suggests that architecture tuned to these cues could serve its occupants at a layer deeper than aesthetics. Sussman's broader argument is that the brain works at walking speed and eye level, hunting for faces, contrast, and activity at the ground floor.

Anjan Chatterjee's lab at the University of Pennsylvania adds nuance to this picture. They summarize architectural experience in three elements: coherence, or how organized and legible a space is; fascination, or how rich in information an environment is; and hominess, or how comfortable it feels. Everyone weighs these differently, but people with an architectural background seem to give coherence more weight than non-architects do. At the same time, he also makes a second point: architects often predict how a building will work, but they rarely collect post-occupancy information to test those predictions.

However, these days, a building lives first as a render, which later gets transferred to a company's social media feed. That matters a lot, because a legible, coherent silhouette that grabs attention is often what the algorithms reward. In some cases, this might even put the architectural brief at risk of becoming a framing exercise: a legible silhouette, a dramatic angle, a frontal moment that survives a person's attention span. In fact, a study of Instagram posts from the Technical University of Munich suggests that architecture is increasingly interacting with social media platforms and, in doing so, taking on their trends and logic. Interestingly, the authors also conclude that spectacle alone does not sustain public interest; popularity is also maintained through function, which depends on repeated documentation of the building's use.

In that sense, the city of Venice in Italy offers an early case study. Photographs of Calatrava's glass-and-steel Ponte della Costituzione are beautiful, but its glass steps proved slippery in the rain, causing people to fall. Finally, years of complaints led the city to consider replacing the glass with stone. The failure was physical rather than perceptual, but it shows the same gap: the picture and the place were judged by different tests, and only one of them was being taken into account before the bridge was built.

Researchers at the Technical University of Denmark describe a performance gap between how buildings are expected to perform and how they actually do; in one of their studies, desk sensors showed that an assumed 100 percent occupancy during design was closer to 70 percent in practice. The tools architects use in their everyday work should close this gap, but they are not able to just yet. BIM software, for example, works like a giant spreadsheet: a database of walls, doors, and quantities that happens to have a 3D view. Dave Lemont, who led Revit's technology before Autodesk acquired it, explained in an ArchDaily interview that moving a wall updates every plan, section, and schedule, while changing a material often sends the team back to specifications, spreadsheets, and drawings, which are changed by hand. But the underlying common ground in this topic is not fragmentation, but rather that the model records what was intended, not what happened after construction.

Therefore, it is possible to see BIM as one more medium that represents a building, while the interesting part could be the shift from representing intent to recording use. Imagine adding the missing column to that spreadsheet: how the building is actually used. Temperature, daylight, noise, density, and anonymized demographics, from every building a firm completes. Because neuroscience is about perception, not just physical conditions, the column would pair those sensor readings with simple occupant feedback on how coherent, engaging, and comfortable a space feels, and with observations of where people actually linger. Over time, this could become a database of what worked, for whom, and in which climate and specific conditions. Architecture's next creative frontier may not be bolder forms, but a humbler habit: go back, measure, and let the building tell you what actually worked.

#8718. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” says Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller says, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, says Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

At the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

An allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.)

By contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran says. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

If you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication before pollen counts rise. That's because antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller says. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.)

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

Whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller says to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

If the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran says. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she says.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller says. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

If you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

#8717. Biscuit-tin lids, horse brasses and scrap metal form sculptural V&A Christmas tree by Burberry

Fashion brand Burberry‘s chief creative officer Daniel Lee worked with artist Ann Carrington to create a Christmas tree sculpture for the Victoria & Albert Museum, made from “memories, traditions and little treasures.”

The 16-foot (4.8-metre) tree, which was unveiled this week, sits in the entrance hall of the Victoria & Albert Museum (VA’s) South Kensington location and was designed to celebrate craft and creativity.

“This collaboration with Ann is a celebration of creativity and what better place to showcase this than the V&A?” Lee said. “It’s one of my favourite museums and a constant source of inspiration to me.”

Lee and Carrington made the tree from old money boxes, biscuit and sweet-tin lids, trinket dishes, silver trays, horse brasses and embossed plates, which were turned into rosettes and ribbons and attached to a metal frame.

The tree, which was made as part of Burberry‘s 170th anniversary celebrations, also features ribbons and bows made of scrap metal.

According to Lee, he and Carrington made the sculpture from “memories, traditions and little treasures. Objects and materials that most people would overlook.”

Carrington added that the design was inspired by the ritual of getting old Christmas decorations out of storage in time for the festive season.

“We wanted to capture that magical moment when you retrieve the battered old box of Christmas decorations from the loft, sift through the faded party bows and tattered tinsel accumulated through the generations and begin the joyful ritual of dressing the tree,” she said.

“I’m always drawn to work that’s handmade, and Ann is a master of her craft,” Lee said of the collaboration.

As well as the tree, the V&A will also be showing The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon, a display that traces the history of the trench coat. Burberry has a multi-year partnership with the museum and is set to open The Burberry Gallery at the South Kensington location in 2028.

Lee has previously unveiled an archive-inspired logo for Burberry, and a few years ago, the brand revealed its redesigned London flagship store.

#8714. Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

Photography by Cyril Marcilhacy. unless stated

Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko has nominated Courage Dzidula Kpodo as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

In this interview he explains why despite growing global attention, his ambitions remain resolutely local.

Having only graduated in 2025 from a master’s in architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) – for which he was awarded the Arthur Rotch Prize for highest overall mark – Kpodo is already someone Lokko believes will “help shape the next chapter of African architecture”.

Kpodo’s work, which sees him blur the roles of architect, artist and archivist, is focused on revealing what he calls the “silences” in prevailing narratives about Ghanaian architecture, and challenging the idea that Ghana’s future development must be a “linear prescription of urbanisation”.

If this sounds theoretical or speculative, Kpodo’s approach is anything but: the site of his MIT thesis was an almost five-acre stretch of farmland in Ghana to which he purchased a 99-year lease in 2022, and is currently using as a live site to consider alternative forms of development in the region.

Stating how, if nothing else, the purchase would “preserve the value of the money I had in my savings account,” Kpodo sees the site becoming an alternative institution of sorts, constructed using materials he has salvaged from vernacular buildings that would otherwise be demolished.

“The committee at MIT was a bit shocked, because they weren’t used to the idea of a thesis project existing in the real world,” Kpodo told Dezeen. “But I still thought of it as almost as a sort of sketch, just at 1:1 scale.”

“Doing that gives you something to test – people are going to interface with it; you can test out its failures and success very quickly.”

Growing up in Kumasi, Kpodo initially focused on visual art in school before pursuing a course in architecture at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), and subsequently MIT.

At KNUST he was quickly exposed to narratives around both architectural success and Ghana’s own architectural history that left him seeking something more “homegrown”.

“We had a lecture from Francis Kéré in which he spoke about his Serpentine Pavilion, and how taking on commissions from big institutions or big clients can become critical for defining your practice,” said Kpodo.

I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come?

“At the time, I couldn’t imagine any of these commissions coming to those of us working in the South. I couldn’t see any architects who were operating on that scale, or even at a kind of global scale,” he continued.

“It almost had the opposite effect on me. I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come? I think it’s by being local that I can have something to offer to the world.”

Kpodo became interested in local architectural archives, initially those of the KNUST Development Office, but also the less formalised collections of images and drawings that he encountered online.

He soon helped establish Postbox Ghana, a research collective initiated by artist Manuela Nebuloni to create an alternative architectural archive using postcards and stamps from the 1950s to the 1980s, which often depicted examples of Tropical Modernism and state infrastructure constructed following Ghana’s independence.

However, Kpodo still felt that these archival materials did not speak to his own understanding of Ghanaian architecture, having grown up in a “not-so-well-to-do context” in Kumasi and only really encountering modernist architecture when first entering the KNUST campus.

“The whole archive that I was exposed to, whether it was in the Development Office or in the postcards, had a huge, significant gap in it,” he said. “I remember stories my dad would tell me about building practices and cultures that just didn’t make it into this archive or our training in architecture school.”

“As a newly independent country, Ghana wanted to break away from any kind of ethnographic notion of what the ‘Gold Coast’ – to use its colonial name – was. So those ‘traditional’ buildings and other forms of practices did not make it into the framework of thinking about what our future meant,” he continued.

“But even though these buildings are far removed from the city centres and from the archive, they were foundational in the sense that they enabled the cocoa industry, and brought in the money that built the institutions and structures that are enshrined in postcards.”

Kpodo began to photograph these vernacular buildings himself, many of them farm structures made using laterite, a type of local red earth that is formed into air and sun-dried blocks for construction

When I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’

Upon finding many of these buildings slated for demolition, Kpodo has more recently begun to purchase them, before carefully deconstructing their laterite structures to become the raw material for new structures on his land.

The idea was initially met locally with some confusion. “I remember one man said, ‘oh, are you going to extract gold from the walls?’ because laterite can contain gold,” he recalled.

“But when I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’ And then some kids would even begin making their own proposals. For me, just creating that imagination is worth it.”

The land that Kpodo purchased in 2022 is in Ghana’s eastern region, and was at the frontier of cocoa production in the early 1900s. Some descendants of the first farmers on the land are still based there, and were among those Kpodo interviewed to understand the history of the landscape.

Alongside the widening of a communal path – the focus of his MIT thesis – and the moving of vernacular building materials there, he has also constructed a simple timber deck, both as a rest point for the farmers and an observation point for watching future changes unfold on the site.

If I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too. You can only do so much in an exhibition setting

Kpodo envisions that this future will include both new agricultural processing facilities for the farmers on the land, as well as community spaces that enable further discussions around its ongoing development.

This work also forms the basis of Kpodo’s educational and curatorial work. He is keen to continue “speaking both languages” – the more practical with the conceptual – but he feels the latter should always be grounded in a “local base” rather than detached from it.

In 2023, his work with Postbox Ghana was exhibited at both Vantage Point Sharjah and the Venice Architecture Biennale. In 2025, he curated the LagosPhoto Biennial alongside Maria Pia Bernardoni and Robin Beth Riskin, with the theme of Incarceration.

Kpodo also taught on the one-month Nomadic African Studio at the African Futures Institute, founded by Lokko as a space “dedicated to rethinking education, culture, and practice from the African continent outward.”

Most recently, he orchestrated the transportation of the wall of a laterite farmhouse a little further afield to the Fondation Cartier in Paris, as part of the exhibition Ibrahim Mahama: Harvest Season, where it is accompanied by images from the Postbox Ghana archives.

“If I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too,” he said. “You can only do so much in an exhibition setting. You can only talk so much. If the work has no ground and no local base, then I think it becomes very difficult for you to bridge what it is that you’re presenting versus the work that it proposes to be doing.”

“We need to cultivate other sites that do the real work, sites that translate it into something which is not necessarily concerned with an educated audience,” he continued.

“My sense is that we’re increasingly going to see the most ‘powerful’ institutions seek out these hyper-local narratives and projects as a way to really understand the world.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

Photography by Cyril Marcilhacy. unless stated

THE ROAD TO WORLD HERITAGE — ARATA ISOZAKI STREETART PLAZA: A Road to World Heritage

THE ROAD TO WORLD HERITAGE — ARATA ISOZAKI STREETART PLAZA: A Road to World Heritage

The name ARATA ISOZAKI STREET expresses our hope that ART PLAZA—the former Oita Prefectural Library designed by Arata Isozaki—will one day be inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. If that hope becomes reality, this street will quite literally become a road leading to a World Heritage site.

#8712. "Intensely physical patterns" cloak Gerhard Richter's self-designed gallery in Doha

Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery.

Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei.

It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter’s own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with Selldorf Architects as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

“My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work,” said Richter.

“The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips,” he continued. “Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”

Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project’s context.

Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf said the design reflects a “profound culmination of many years of [Richter’s] research into abstraction”.

“I am grateful for the welcome that Gerhard Richter extended to me, and for the wonderful dialogue that ensued, as my studio made manifest the work that had existed in his mind,” she said.

“This pavilion is the profound culmination of many years of his research into abstraction, with intensely physical patterns that invite you to immerse yourself in their endlessness,” she continued.

“The more I look at them, the more fascinating they become to me as an architectural space to experience.”

Inside, Richter’s paintings and sculptures are displayed throughout the hexagonal gallery space. This includes both archival and new works made especially for the pavilion.

Among the new works is the Strip Tower – a freestanding tripartite sculpture.

The opening of Doha Pavilion coincides with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, which is an international visual arts quadrennial.

Elsewhere, Selldorf Architects recently completed the controversial remodel of the National Gallery’s Sainsbury Wing. In an interview with Dezeen after the opening, founder Selldorf said that “what matters is I know why we did things”.
